newsitem.title: GREECE: Skipped auction of Greek T-bills a setback- market.
newsitem.headline: Skipped auction of Greek T-bills a setback- market.

text.p: Greek and foreign bankers hammered the finance ministry's decision not to auction the 12-month T-bill on February 28 calling it a setback that would adversely affect foreign demand for floating rate notes in the future.

"An opportunity was missed for a substantial new interest rate reduction on government titles that would be forthcoming from foreign demand if basis risk was dealt with," said Harris Makkas, deputy general manager at BankAmerica, Athens.
The finance ministry said on Wednesday it would issue 12-month T-bills and two-year zero coupon bonds on February 28 without specifying interest rates.

The benchmark 12-month T-bill interest rate plus a spread is used to refix coupons on FRNs. Market players have long complained about the basis risk involved in setting the 12-month T-bill administratively and the subsequent risk premium factored into FRN prices.

"I am disappointed about the decision. I was under the impression that auctions of 12-month T-bills would become normal practice from now on," said a London-based bond dealer. "This will definitely influence my decision to buy into Greek FRNs in the future."
The dealer echoed a similar disappointment expressed by U.S-based fund managers who were among the largest foreign buyers of Greek FRNs.
"I am very disappointed with the setback," said the asset manager of a U.S-based fund.
Greece auctioned 300 billion drachmas of 12-month T-bills on February 3 with the base rate set at 10.90 percent producing an average accepted price of 90.15.

The auction created havoc in the market because the finance ministry did not notify all credit institutions at the same time of its last minute decision to give bidding banks a gross commission of 0.45 percent.
It was the second auction of 12-month T-bills since the summer of 1995.
Other local dealers said they were let down by the finance ministry's decision but were not surprised.
"It is a negative development but I am not surprised given the past history of decision-making at the finance ministry," said a senior bond dealer at a foreign bank.

Some market players said skipping the auction of 12-month T-bills revealed some lingering doubts on the part of the finance ministry over the sustainability of falling yields should it allow the market to set them.

Ministry officials have said in the past that setting interest rates on 12-month T-bills administratively served the interests of local retail investors who were the most faithful fans of the debt instrument but were not sophisticated enough. --Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
